newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador Congress begins discussion on Bucaram fate.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador Congress begins discussion on Bucaram fate.

text.p: Ecuador's Congress began an extraordinary session late on Thursday to debate the possible ousting of President Abdala Bucaram who threatened to crush any unconstitutional moves against him.
The session began on the second day of a 48-hour general strike called by unions to oppose government austerity measures.

"The country has already said that we not only need to change a few persons or roll back a few measures. They said we need a new government and we have to abide by that," said Franklin Vergara of the opposition Social Christian Party.
The government issued a statement saying the Congress session was unconstitutional as it had not been advertised in local newspapers.

In an address to the nation, Bucaram said: "The government makes clear that in the case of an attempt to break with constitutional order, I will assume all the powers available to protect the legitimacy of the popular will and the national judicial order."
Outside Congress at least two people were injured by gunshots as 4,000 demonstrators called on legislators to dismiss Bucaram.

An unknown number of the protesters, angered by the gunfire, threw rocks and molotov cocktails at security forces guarding Congress. After police responded with teargas, the protest quickly dissipated, Radio Quito reported.
A Congress spokesman identified one of the injured as a spokesman for a political party, the Popular Democratic Movement. The other, said Radio Quito, was a local newspaper photographer.
Bucaram announced earlier he was reshuffling his cabinet and said he would reconsider steep rises in the rates of public services, which led to the general strike and triggered social unrest.
Bucaram said he was reviewing price hikes in gas and electricity prices and would freeze fuel prices.

He also announced he had accepted the resignation of his controversial Energy and Mining Minister Alfredo Adum as part of a cabinet shakeup. Government Minister Frank Vargas, Social Welfare Minister Adolfo Bucaram, who is the president's brother, and Administration Secretary Miguel Salem, were also leaving.
"I will carry out a broad renewal of officials and relations in order to tune in to the needs of the country," Bucaram said.
Unions earlier announced they had decided to indefinitely extend the 48-hour general strike they began on Wednesday until they succeeded in pushing Bucaram out of his job.

"In a meeting at dawn, we decided to harden our stance and continue the strike until we achieve the dismissal of Abdala Bucaram," the Coordinating Board for Social Protests and the Indigenous People's Confederation said in a statement.
Social unrest erupted in the Andean country of 11.7 million people in January when the government launched an austerity package including hikes in electricity, telephone and public transport rates.

The appointment by Bucaram of some friends and family members to key posts and his flamboyant personality has also irritated his opponents. Nicknamed "El Loco" -- "madman" in Spanish -- he released a rock-and-roll record soon after taking office and his antics included shaving his moustache off live on television.
A top Bucaram supporter said the government was lobbying Congress hard to avoid a vote to oust the president.
"We are putting together a majority. We are sure we are going to make it," said Monetary Board president Alvaro Noboa.

But one opposition congressman, Luis Macas, of the Pachakutik-New Country Party, said he was determined to vote to overthrow Bucaram, despite the president's warnings he might assume extra powers if faced with a rebellious Congress.
"Our position is definitely to declare the post of president of Ecuador vacant," Macas told Reuters.
Of Congress's 82 members, 19 belong to Bucaram's Roldosista Party, while another 12 are government allies.

Government sources said 55 congressmen would have to vote for Bucaram to be fired to depose him, but opposition members said they would only need 42 votes. If Congress did vote to remove Bucaram, the post of president would be declared vacant.
